clue_text: Michel Foucault's dispatches on the Iranian Revolution ran in the Italian daily Corriere della Sera; this left-of-center Paris weekly carried some of them as well.

distractor_rationales.why_plausible: The leading French daily, and the other French paper that carried his Iran pieces.
distractor_rationales.why_wrong: It is a daily; the weekly that ran them was Le Nouvel Observateur.

distractor_rationales.why_plausible: Sartre's left review, the obvious Paris home for a philosopher's political writing.
distractor_rationales.why_wrong: A monthly founded by Sartre and Beauvoir, and it did not carry these pieces.

distractor_rationales.why_plausible: The French Communist daily, the loudest left voice in Paris.
distractor_rationales.why_wrong: A party daily, not the left-of-center weekly that published him.

explanation: Foucault placed part of his Iran writings in French outlets too, among them the left-of-center weekly Le Nouvel Observateur and the daily Le Monde.
book_title: Foucault and the Iranian Revolution: Gender and the Seductions of Islamism
author: Janet Afary and Kevin B. Anderson
chapter: Appendix: Foucault and His Critics, an Annotated Transl
supporting_passage: Foucault published a smaller but not insigniﬁcant portion of his writings on Iran in several French publications, including the left-of-center weekly Le Nouvel Observateur and the leading newspaper Le Monde.

host_reactions.correct_generic: Le Nouvel Observateur. It ran Foucault's Iran dispatches beside Le Monde's; a revolution always reads better in French.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: A Paris paper with a bigger circulation than the one that bought him, and no Foucault in it. Right city, wrong shelf.

clue_text: Even many members and cadres of the Tudeh Party balked at giving unconditional support to the measures of this man's Democratic Party.

distractor_rationales.why_plausible: A long-serving Tudeh leader and the party's first secretary.
distractor_rationales.why_wrong: He led the Tudeh from Tehran; the Democratic Party of Azerbaijan was Pishevari's.

distractor_rationales.why_plausible: One of the best-known Tudeh cadres of the era.
distractor_rationales.why_wrong: A party functionary, not the founder of the Azerbaijan Democratic Party.

distractor_rationales.why_plausible: A senior Tudeh leader schooled in Soviet politics.
distractor_rationales.why_wrong: A Tudeh man; the man whose party the Tudeh would not fully endorse was Pishevari.

explanation: Tudeh members and cadres could not bring themselves to give unconditional support to the measures of Pishevari's Democratic Party in Azerbaijan.

author: Homa Katouzian and Hossein Shahidi
chapter: From multilingual empire to modern state
supporting_passage: many members and cadres of the Tudeh party to give their unconditional support to the measures taken by Pishevari’s Democratic Party.

host_reactions.correct_generic: Ja'far Pishevari. He ran Soviet-blessed Azerbaijan with a party the Tudeh's own members would not fully sign on to; comrades can be so particular.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: Those names belong to the Tudeh's own leadership. The party the rank and file shied away from belonged to one man, and you have not named him.

clue_text: The Shahnameh gives Turan, Iran's enemy, a capital by this name, though no one has ever located the site of the town.

distractor_rationales.why_plausible: The great Silk Road city of Transoxiana, the heart of the land the poem calls Turan.
distractor_rationales.why_wrong: A real, excavated city; the capital the poem names was never located.

distractor_rationales.why_plausible: Another fabled Transoxianan city, long the seat of Iranianate dynasties.
distractor_rationales.why_wrong: Bukhara's site is known; Gang Dezh's is not.

distractor_rationales.why_plausible: A great oasis metropolis of Khurasan and a byword for Central Asian grandeur.
distractor_rationales.why_wrong: Merv is thoroughly excavated; the poem's Turanian capital left nothing to dig.

explanation: The poem names Turan's capital Gang Dezh, a place that has never been matched to any known site.
book_title: Iran Facing Others: Identity Boundaries in a Historical Perspective
author: Abbas Amanat and Farzin Vejdani
chapter: 1 Iran and Aniran: The Shaping of a Legend
supporting_passage: Strangely enough we do learn the name of the capital of Iran's enemy, Turan, which is referred to as “Gang Dezh,” although the site of this town, if it was a town, has never been historically identified.

host_reactions.correct_generic: Gang Dezh. The Shahnameh knew exactly where Turan kept its throne; the archaeologists never found it, and they looked.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: Real cities, every one of them, with real ruins. That is precisely what rules them out.

clue_text: In 1976 the Pahlavi state named Iran's first woman ambassador and posted her to this country.

distractor_rationales.why_plausible: A Scandinavian posting, the sort of modern, unthreatening capital a showcase appointment would get.
distractor_rationales.why_wrong: The first woman ambassador went to Copenhagen.

distractor_rationales.why_plausible: Stockholm was another favored Nordic post for the Shah's diplomatic showcase.
distractor_rationales.why_wrong: Not the capital that received her.

distractor_rationales.why_plausible: A small, progressive European capital of the kind Tehran liked for a first.
distractor_rationales.why_wrong: The posting was Danish, not Dutch.

explanation: Iran's first woman ambassador was sent to Denmark in 1976, one of the throne's late payments on women's advancement.
author: Deniz Kandiyoti
chapter: Hazards of Modernity and Morality: Women, State and Ide
supporting_passage: Her own appointment as Iran's first female ambassador (to Denmark) in 1976

host_reactions.correct_generic: Denmark. Copenhagen got Iran's first woman ambassador, and the court took the credit; a throne is generous with what it never gave up.
host_reactions.wrong_generic: Cold, European and plausible, all three of them, which is the trap. The throne reached into its pocket for exactly one country.
